html:
The Ãwa, better known as the Avá-Canoeiro, are a Tupi-Guarani people of the upper Tocantins and Araguaia rivers in central Brazil, in today's Goiás and Tocantins. The Portuguese name means "canoe people".

When the gold rush brought miners and ranchers into Goiás in the 1700s, the Avá-Canoeiro fought back and were hunted in return. For two centuries they survived by hiding in small, mobile bands, and they became one of the most persecuted peoples of colonial Brazil and the empire after it. Small groups were contacted only in the 1970s and 1980s, some near the Ilha do Bananal among the Karajá and Javaé. Only a few dozen remain, and their Tupian language is endangered.
